title: Job 14:1–12
context: Job continues the reply he began in 12:1, now turning from his friends to address God directly. He reflects on the brevity and trouble of human life, asks why God should bring so frail a creature into judgment, and contrasts a cut-down tree, which can sprout again, with a man who lies down and does not rise. The speaker throughout is Job, and his words are a lament spoken in suffering, not a settled doctrinal statement.

verses.text: “Man, who is born of a woman, is of few days, and full of trouble.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says that man, born of a woman, is of few days and full of trouble. Arminian readers hear a sufferer naming the shared frailty of every human life, and they see honesty about pain as part of faithful lament.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job’s words echo the Psalms on human brevity (Psalm 90:10). Spoken by Job from within his suffering, the verse is a cry of experience rather than a formal teaching about human nature.

verses.text: He grows up like a flower, and is cut down. He also flees like a shadow, and doesn’t continue.
verses.arminianNotes: Job compares a man to a flower cut down and a shadow that flees. Arminian readers see the image as Job’s vivid sense of how quickly life passes, sharpened by his own losses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that similar images of fading grass and flowers appear in Psalm 103:15-16 and Isaiah 40:6-8. Job uses them to stress that human life cannot hold its place.

verses.text: Do you open your eyes on such a one, and bring me into judgment with you?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether God really fixes his eyes on such a frail creature to bring him into judgment. Arminian readers see a bold, honest complaint addressed directly to God rather than about him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Job’s question assumes God’s attention and justice even as he protests them. The complaint is framed as a plea within relationship, not a rejection of God.

verses.text: Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one.
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks, Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one. Arminian readers note that many later readers have connected this with inherited corruption, while Job’s own point concerns human frailty before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often cite the verse in discussions of native corruption, as the Psalms 51:5 box discusses. In context, Job is pleading for leniency because of human weakness, not building a doctrine.

verses.text: Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months is with you, and you have appointed his bounds that he can’t pass.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says man’s days are determined and his bounds appointed by God. Arminian readers hear Job acknowledging God’s authority over life’s span; the Psalms 139:16 box discusses how the traditions understand God’s knowledge of our days.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job confessing that the length of life lies in God’s hands. He states this not as comfort but as part of his plea that God would leave so limited a creature alone.

verses.text: Look away from him, that he may rest, until he accomplishes, as a hireling, his day.
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks God to look away so that man may rest until he finishes his day like a hired worker. Arminian readers hear a weary sufferer longing for relief rather than constant scrutiny.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job pictures life as hard labor and asks only for a break before its end. The hireling image recalls his earlier complaint in 7:1-2.

verses.text: “For there is hope for a tree if it is cut down, that it will sprout again, that the tender branch of it will not cease.
verses.arminianNotes: Job observes that there is hope for a tree that is cut down, for it will sprout again. Arminian readers see Job reaching for an image of renewal even while contrasting it with human death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the word hope here sets up the contrast that follows. Nature seems to offer a second chance that Job cannot yet see for human beings.

verses.text: Though its root grows old in the earth, and its stock dies in the ground,
verses.arminianNotes: Though the tree’s root grows old and its stump dies in the ground, it can still revive. Arminian readers see Job dwelling on the stubborn life of a tree to sharpen his sense of human loss.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the detail of the aging root and dying stump. Job describes a situation that looks hopeless, yet life remains hidden within it.

verses.text: yet through the scent of water it will bud, and sprout boughs like a plant.
verses.arminianNotes: Through the scent of water, the stump buds and sends out boughs. Arminian readers see the tenderness of the image, a picture of life returning at the smallest touch of grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Isaiah later uses the image of a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1). In Job’s speech, however, the tree serves as a contrast, not a promise.

verses.text: But man dies, and is laid low. Yes, man gives up the spirit, and where is he?
verses.arminianNotes: But man dies and is laid low; he gives up the spirit, and where is he? Arminian readers hear Job’s honest question about what lies beyond death, voiced without easy answers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast with the tree made explicit. Job’s question, where is he?, expresses the darkness of death as he experiences it, not a final statement about the afterlife.

verses.text: As the waters fail from the sea, and the river wastes and dries up,
verses.arminianNotes: As waters fail from the sea and a river dries up, so human life disappears. Arminian readers see Job choosing images of loss that cannot be reversed by human effort.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image of drying waters stresses finality. Job speaks as one who sees no natural process that could restore a dead man.

verses.text: so man lies down and doesn’t rise. Until the heavens are no more, they will not awake, nor be roused out of their sleep.
verses.arminianNotes: Man lies down and does not rise; until the heavens are no more, they will not awake. Arminian readers note that some read until the heavens are no more as an idiom for never, while others see a hint of a limit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the language of sleep and waking has invited later readers to think of resurrection, but in Job’s mouth the verse stresses that the dead do not return in the ordinary course of things.
